title: The community garden
summary: Khám phá một khu vườn nhỏ và thay đổi lớn trong khu phố.
passage: A. There used to be an empty piece of land behind East Street Library. People walked past it on their way to work, but nobody stopped there. In March, a group of neighbours asked the council if they could use the land to grow vegetables. The council agreed to lend it to them for three years. The neighbours did not have to pay rent, but they had to keep the area clean and open to everyone during the day.

B. The first job was to remove rubbish. Twenty volunteers came on a Saturday morning, including two people who had never grown a plant before. A local shop gave them tools, and the library put a notice in its window asking for seeds. By the end of April, there were rows of carrots and beans. The group collected rainwater in large containers because there was no tap in the garden.

C. Now the garden opens at nine each morning. Visitors can sit on wooden benches, and children have a small area where they grow flowers. The volunteers share the vegetables rather than sell them. They say the most important result is that neighbours have started talking to one another. They hope to build a small shelter next year so that people can still meet when it rains.

title: Libraries without walls
summary: Thư viện hiện đại mở rộng vai trò như thế nào?
passage: A. When the library in Westford announced that it would lend sewing machines, the response was mixed. Some residents welcomed the idea; others wondered whether the institution was forgetting its purpose. For librarian Maya Collins, however, a library has always been about access. Books are one way of sharing knowledge, but they are not the only way. A resident who borrows a machine and learns to repair a jacket has gained a practical skill without buying expensive equipment.

B. Before expanding the service, staff carried out a survey. They expected requests for cameras and computer equipment. Those items were popular, but gardening tools attracted even more interest. The library therefore began with a small collection of tools and ran free demonstrations on Saturday afternoons. It did not purchase everything that people requested. Equipment that required specialist supervision was excluded, and every item had to fit into the existing storage room.

C. The project brought challenges. Returned items needed checking, and the original booking system could not manage objects that had several separate parts. Staff developed a checklist and allowed extra time between loans. Although maintaining the collection takes work, fewer items have been damaged than expected. A university team is now measuring whether borrowers buy less equipment themselves. Early interviews suggest that people value the chance to try something before deciding whether to own it.

D. The library still spends most of its budget on reading materials. Collins argues that the new collection supports that work rather than replacing it. Someone who attends a repair workshop may later borrow a book about design. The building has become a place where readers, makers and people looking for advice meet. Whether the model can succeed in smaller libraries will depend on available staff time, storage and local demand.

title: The cooling power of trees
summary: Đọc bằng chứng về tán cây, nhiệt độ và lựa chọn quy hoạch.
passage: A. On a summer afternoon, the difference between a tree-lined street and a bare car park can be striking. Shade blocks solar radiation, while water released through leaves removes heat from the surrounding air. These processes are well understood, yet predicting the cooling effect of a particular planting scheme remains difficult. The result depends on the size and health of trees, the arrangement of buildings and the availability of water. A single figure describing the benefit of urban trees can therefore be misleading.

B. Researchers in the fictional city of Mereton installed temperature sensors along twelve streets. Rather than comparing neighbourhood averages, they placed instruments at the height of a pedestrian's head. Streets with continuous tree cover were generally cooler during the afternoon, but the difference narrowed after sunset. The researchers cautioned that their study covered only one summer. It demonstrated a local pattern, not a universal promise that the same planting plan would produce identical results elsewhere.

C. Choosing a species involves trade-offs. A fast-growing tree may create shade quickly but require considerable water. A drought-tolerant species may survive with less irrigation while developing a smaller canopy. Underground pipes, narrow pavements and maintenance budgets can limit what is feasible. Planners increasingly favour a mixture of species: diversity reduces the risk that a single disease will remove an entire street's shade. It also makes maintenance less predictable because different trees need attention at different times.

D. Distribution matters as much as the number of trees planted. In many cities, areas with the highest temperatures also have the least canopy cover. If new planting goes mainly to locations where residents can contribute money, existing inequalities may deepen. Mereton's council consequently prioritised routes used by people walking to schools and clinics. Its programme included funding for watering young trees over several years. Announcing how many trees had been planted would have been easier than checking how many survived, but survival was the measure the council chose.

E. Trees cannot solve every problem associated with extreme heat. Reflective roofs, ventilation, accessible drinking water and shaded public spaces remain important. The evidence supports incorporating trees into a wider strategy rather than treating planting as a substitute for other measures. A successful programme combines realistic biological expectations with a clear account of who will benefit and who will maintain the trees.

title: The paradox of predictable cities
summary: Phân tích lập luận về dữ liệu, mô hình và hành vi đô thị.
passage: A. Urban models promise to turn the apparent disorder of city life into patterns that can inform decisions. Passenger movements, energy demand and deliveries all generate records from which recurring relationships can be inferred. The temptation is to regard a sufficiently detailed model as a transparent window onto the city itself. Yet a model is a selective description: its categories determine which activities become visible and which are treated as noise. Increasing the volume of observations does not remove that selection.

B. Consider a transport model calibrated against trips recorded by a mobile application. If people who travel infrequently or cannot afford reliable mobile data are underrepresented, the model may underestimate demand along the routes they use. The resulting timetable can then discourage those journeys further. What began as a measurement gap becomes an apparent confirmation of the original estimate. The difficulty is not simply that the sample is incomplete; the decisions informed by the sample can reshape the behaviour being measured.

C. This feedback does not make prediction useless. It changes what a responsible prediction must disclose. A forecast of passenger numbers under an unchanged timetable answers a different question from a forecast under improved service. Combining the two without stating the assumption gives an illusion of certainty. Some planning teams now publish several scenarios and explain which decisions could cause outcomes to diverge. Critics sometimes describe this as indecision, although an explicit range may be more informative than a single precise number whose conditions remain hidden.

D. A further complication concerns the difference between accuracy and usefulness. A model may reproduce the total number of journeys with impressive precision while distributing them incorrectly between neighbourhoods. For a budget overview, the aggregate may be adequate. For deciding where to add a bus stop, it is inadequate. Evaluation therefore needs to be tied to the decision at hand. There is no context-free score that guarantees a model will serve every planning purpose equally well.

E. Participatory approaches offer one response. Residents can identify missing routes, informal services and barriers that numerical records fail to capture. Their accounts do not automatically resolve disputes: participants may have conflicting interests, and the most vocal group may not represent everyone. Nevertheless, treating such accounts as evidence rather than decorative consultation can reveal assumptions before they become embedded in infrastructure. Quantitative and qualitative methods are complementary when each is allowed to challenge the other's categories.

F. The paradox is that a useful model may make its own initial prediction obsolete. If a warning about overcrowding leads to additional services, the forecast crowding may never occur. Judging the warning solely by its failure to materialise would confuse a successful intervention with a defective forecast. Models should thus be assessed not only as descriptions of a fixed world but as participants in a changing one. Their value lies in supporting accountable decisions, including decisions that alter the patterns from which the models were built.

title: A visit to Riverside Centre
summary: Nghe thông tin đăng ký, thời gian và vật dụng cho lớp học.
transcript: Welcome to Riverside Community Centre. This message gives information about our beginner photography course. The course starts on Monday, the fourteenth of May, and runs for six weeks. Classes begin at half past six in the evening and finish at eight. Please arrive ten minutes before the first class so that we can check your registration. The class meets in room twelve, on the first floor, next to the small library. There is a lift near the entrance. You do not need an expensive camera. A phone with a camera is enough for the first two lessons. After that, the centre can lend you a camera if you would like to try one. Please bring a notebook to every class. The fee for the whole course is forty pounds. This includes a printed workbook, but it does not include refreshments. Tea and coffee are available in the cafe downstairs. If you cycle to the centre, you can leave your bicycle behind the building. Car parking is limited, so we recommend using the number seven bus. To reserve a place, call our office before Friday. We look forward to meeting you.

title: Planning the coastal walk
summary: Theo dõi lịch trình chuyến đi và các thay đổi khi lập kế hoạch.
transcript: Thanks for joining this briefing about Saturday's coastal walk. There have been a few changes since we sent out the leaflet, so please listen carefully. We originally planned to meet outside the railway station at nine, but engineering work means there will be replacement buses that morning. We will now meet at the entrance to the town museum at nine thirty. The coach will leave ten minutes later. Our first stop is the old lighthouse. A guide will explain how it was built, although we will not be allowed to climb the tower because repair work is still taking place. From there we will walk along the cliff path. It is a fairly gentle route, but some sections can be slippery. Walking boots are recommended; ordinary trainers may not give enough support. Lunch will be at a sheltered picnic area near the harbour. The cafe there is closed for the season, so everyone must bring a packed lunch. Please also carry at least a litre of water. In the afternoon, we will visit the small wildlife centre. We had hoped to include a boat trip, but the forecast wind is too strong. Instead, a volunteer will lead a session on identifying coastal birds. We should return to the museum by five. If the weather deteriorates badly, we will telephone participants on Friday evening. Otherwise, assume the walk is going ahead. Our office number is printed at the bottom of your booking confirmation.

title: Researching student study spaces
summary: Nghe nhận xét của giảng viên về phương pháp khảo sát.
transcript: I have read your proposal about student study spaces, and the topic is promising. I would like you to make the research question more specific, though. At the moment you ask whether students like the library. That is too broad. A better question might be how the availability of quiet areas affects the length of students' visits. Your plan to distribute an online questionnaire is sensible, but do not rely on it alone. Students who rarely use the library may never see the announcement. Try brief interviews near the main entrance as well as in the student cafe. You will still have a convenience sample, and you should acknowledge that limitation. I noticed you intend to record noise levels every morning. That will miss the busiest period, which is usually early afternoon. Take measurements at three different times of day, and keep the location of your instrument consistent. You do not need to buy a specialist device; the department has one you can borrow. As for your interview questions, avoid asking whether people agree that the library is too noisy. That wording already suggests the answer. Ask them to describe their experience first. Later, you can invite them to compare the library with other places they study. Finally, be realistic about what the results can establish. A relationship between noise and shorter visits would not prove that noise caused students to leave. They may have arrived for a short visit in the first place. A short observational study can identify patterns worth investigating, but it cannot settle every question. Please revise the sampling section and send it to me by Wednesday.

title: When memory meets evidence
summary: Nghe bài giảng học thuật về ký ức, độ tự tin và bằng chứng.
transcript: Today I want to examine a distinction that is easy to overlook: the difference between confidence in a memory and the accuracy of that memory. Vivid recollection can feel like direct access to an event, but remembering is a reconstructive activity. We retrieve fragments and interpret them using what we know now. This does not mean that every memory is false. It means that the subjective feeling of certainty is not, on its own, a reliable test of precision. In one hypothetical experiment, participants watch a short film of a street scene. They are later asked questions containing either neutral wording or a misleading suggestion. Some participants subsequently report seeing an object mentioned only in the question. The important point is not that people are careless. Information encountered after an event can become difficult to distinguish from information encountered during it. Repetition creates another complication. Rehearsing a particular account may make it easier to retrieve, increasing confidence without introducing any new evidence. If a group repeatedly discusses the same account, agreement can emerge even when members originally remembered different details. Researchers therefore distinguish independent corroboration from simple repetition. Five reports do not necessarily provide five independent sources. What practical conclusions follow? First, record initial accounts before witnesses discuss them together. Second, avoid questions that embed an expected answer. Third, preserve uncertainty in the record rather than translating hesitant language into an apparently definitive statement. None of these measures guarantees perfect recall. Their purpose is to reduce avoidable contamination and make the remaining uncertainty visible. Finally, consider how we evaluate corrections. A witness who revises a detail after seeing new evidence may appear less trustworthy than someone who never changes their story. Yet appropriate revision can demonstrate responsiveness to evidence. Consistency is useful only when we understand how it was produced. Our task is not to reward confidence, but to examine the conditions under which a claim was formed.

questions.prompt: What is the lecturer's central distinction?
options: A feeling of certainty differs from demonstrated accuracy.

options: They may not be independent sources.
